questions.stem: West African Traditional Religion is passed from one generation to the next mainly through
questions.explanation: W.A.T.R. has no written scripture; beliefs are handed down orally and through rituals and everyday life.

questions.stem: A farmer in a Bini village pours libation before clearing new land and asks the elders for the right day to plant. This shows that in W.A.T.R.
options: religion is limited to the shrine
only priests may own and clear farmland
religion touches every part of life
worship takes place once a year
questions.explanation: Traditional religion is not separated from work, family or politics; it permeates all of life.

questions.topic: Purpose of the study of W.A.T.R.
questions.stem: Chidi says that studying W.A.T.R. in school has helped him respect his grandparents' customs. This shows that one purpose of the study is to
options: make every pupil join a village shrine
questions.explanation: The study helps learners appreciate their heritage and the values of their society.

questions.topic: Terms Used to Describe West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: The word 'fetish', once used by European writers for African religion, came originally from a
questions.explanation: 'Fetish' derives from the Portuguese 'feitico', meaning a made thing or charm.

questions.topic: Terms Used to Describe West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: E. Bolaji Idowu described the Yoruba belief in one Supreme God who works through many divinities as
questions.explanation: Idowu used 'diffused monotheism' for belief in one God whose authority is shared out among divinities.

questions.stem: The bronze and terracotta heads found at Ife are useful to the student of W.A.T.R. mainly as
options: written records of the prayers of priests
questions.explanation: Works of art are non-oral sources that reflect beliefs about kingship and the sacred.

questions.stem: The saying 'When the lizard nods its head, it is not saying yes to the hawk' is useful to a student of W.A.T.R. as an example of
questions.explanation: Proverbs carry religious and moral ideas and are an important oral source.

questions.topic: Approaches to the Study of West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: A researcher who describes a festival exactly as worshippers experience it, without judging whether their beliefs are true, is using the
questions.explanation: Phenomenology describes religion as it appears to believers and suspends judgement.

questions.stem: Among the Igbo, the Supreme Being is commonly called
questions.explanation: Chukwu (also Chineke) is the Igbo name; Olodumare is Yoruba, Onyame Akan, Mawu Ewe, Soko Nupe.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a condition for becoming an ancestor in W.A.T.R.?
options: Being a stranger in the town
questions.explanation: Ancestors must have lived well, reached old age, had children, died a good death and received proper burial.

questions.stem: In Yoruba belief, the divinity of iron, war and hunting is
questions.explanation: Ogun is god of iron; Sango of thunder; Orunmila of wisdom and divination; Obatala of moulding humans.

questions.stem: The Igbo earth goddess, guardian of morality and fertility, is
questions.explanation: Ala (Ani) is the Igbo earth goddess; Asase Yaa is the Akan earth goddess.

questions.stem: An amulet differs from many other charms in that it is mainly
questions.explanation: Amulets are protective objects worn or kept on the person.

questions.stem: At a family meeting, an elder pours gin on the ground and calls the names of departed grandfathers. The rite he performs is called
questions.explanation: Libation is the ritual pouring of liquid as an offering.

questions.stem: A sacrifice offered in W.A.T.R. to remove the guilt of a broken taboo is
questions.explanation: Propitiatory (expiatory) sacrifices appease an offended spirit and remove guilt.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of worship in W.A.T.R.?
questions.explanation: There is no written creed in W.A.T.R.

questions.topic: Religious Personalities in West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: The Akan priest or priestess who serves a divinity and may be possessed by it is the
questions.explanation: The okomfo is the Akan priest(ess) of a divinity.

questions.topic: Festivals in West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: Homowo, celebrated by the Ga of Ghana, is a festival that
options: marks the death of a king
questions.explanation: Homowo means 'hooting at hunger' and recalls a past famine.

questions.topic: Festivals in West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: In many Igbo communities, a person who eats new yams before the New Yam festival has been performed is regarded as having
questions.explanation: The festival must precede the eating of new yams; eating them earlier offends the earth and ancestors.

questions.stem: In W.A.T.R. a sick person is often taken to a diviner first because illness is believed to
questions.explanation: Traditional thought looks for spiritual causes behind sickness.

questions.stem: Villagers in a remote community prefer roots and leaves from the bush to tablets from the city mainly because the herbs
options: are cheap and close at hand
questions.explanation: Herbs are cheap and close at hand, though dosage and hygiene can be problems.

questions.stem: A government plan to bring herbalists into primary health care would have to tackle first the problem of
questions.explanation: Dosages are not measured uniformly, which can endanger patients.

questions.stem: John Mbiti argued that the traditional African concept of time is mainly
options: a present and a long past
questions.explanation: Mbiti's Sasa and Zamani describe time as a present and a long past, with little emphasis on the distant future.

questions.stem: In W.A.T.R., wealth gained through ritual killing is regarded as
options: a mark of a good destiny
questions.explanation: Wealth must be honestly gained; ritual money brings shame and punishment.

questions.stem: Among the Akan, the part of a person believed to come directly from God and to return to Him at death is the
questions.explanation: The okra is the life-soul from Onyame; mogya is blood from the mother, ntoro from the father.

questions.stem: The Yoruba belief that each person chooses a destiny before birth is linked with the
questions.explanation: Ori, the inner head, carries the destiny chosen before birth.

questions.stem: In W.A.T.R., witches are mainly believed to
options: heal the sick with herbs and incantations
questions.explanation: Witches are feared as enemies of life who cause harm by spiritual power.

questions.stem: A child believed to be born, to die and to be reborn repeatedly to the same mother is called ogbanje by the Igbo and, by the Yoruba,
questions.explanation: Abiku is the Yoruba equivalent of the Igbo ogbanje.

questions.topic: Religion and Ethics in West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: In W.A.T.R., the moral code is maintained mainly through
options: written constitutions and courts of appeal
taboos and fear of the divinities
questions.explanation: Taboos, sanctions of the divinities and ancestors and communal pressure keep morality.

questions.topic: Stages of the rites of passage
questions.stem: The correct order of the rites of passage is
questions.explanation: Life is marked in order from birth to initiation/puberty, marriage and death.

questions.stem: A major importance of the puberty or initiation rite is that it
options: ends a person's membership of the family
questions.explanation: Initiation teaches the young the values and duties of adulthood.

questions.stem: The Golden Stool of the Asante is believed to contain
options: the bones of the first king
the wealth of all the chiefs
the laws given by the British
the soul of the Asante nation
the tools of the first blacksmith
questions.explanation: The Sika Dwa Kofi is held to embody the spirit and unity of the Asante people.

questions.stem: Among the Fante, Asafo companies traditionally served as
questions.explanation: Asafo companies were warrior bands that also performed civic and ritual duties.

questions.stem: The Ogbunike Caves, a sacred site that draws many visitors, are found in
questions.explanation: The Ogbunike Caves are in Oyi area of Anambra State and are held sacred by the local people.

questions.stem: Which of the following best shows how traditional religion can benefit the economy through tourism?
options: Sacred groves are cleared for farms
questions.explanation: Festivals and sacred sites attract tourists whose spending creates income for local people.

questions.stem: Tourists who visit a royal palace to see a carved ancestral stool are attracted mainly by a
questions.explanation: Stools, masks and shrines are sacred objects of interest to tourists.

questions.topic: Religion and Stress Management in West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem: A trader who is troubled after losing her goods visits a diviner, who advises a sacrifice and assures her of the ancestors' support. This shows W.A.T.R. helping in
questions.explanation: Divination, sacrifice and reassurance relieve anxiety and help people cope with stress.

questions.stem: A traditional taboo that forbids a nursing mother to resume sexual relations too soon after childbirth helps mainly to
options: space births for the mother's health
questions.explanation: Post-partum abstinence spaces births and protects the health of mother and child.

questions.stem: Health workers today campaign against female circumcision mainly because it
options: is too costly for most families to perform
can cause bleeding and childbirth problems
questions.explanation: Female genital cutting can cause haemorrhage, infection and complications at childbirth.

questions.stem: Which of the following has most weakened the influence of W.A.T.R. in modern West Africa?
questions.explanation: Western education, urbanisation and the spread of other religions have reduced its hold.

questions.topic: Terms Used to Describe West African Traditional Religion
questions.stem:
(a) Explain why each of the following terms is considered inappropriate for describing West African Traditional Religion: (i) paganism (ii) fetishism (iii) juju. [9 marks]
(b) State three terms that scholars now prefer or accept in describing the religion. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: paganism - wrongly suggests a primitive or godless religion of villagers, ignoring belief in God
3 marks: fetishism - from Portuguese 'feitico'; treats the religion as worship of objects and ignores its beliefs and values
3 marks: juju - a vague, derogatory word for charms; reduces the religion to magic
6 marks: any three accepted terms, 2 marks each - West African Traditional Religion, African Traditional Religion, indigenous religion, diffused monotheism (Idowu)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Each label came from outsiders who misunderstood the religion. 'Paganism' meant the faith of rustic people and implies no knowledge of God; 'fetishism' comes from the Portuguese feitico and pictures worshippers as adoring objects; 'juju' is a loose word for charms that reduces the religion to magic. Scholars now prefer 'West African Traditional Religion', 'indigenous religion', or describe its structure as 'diffused monotheism'.

questions.stem:
(a) Give the names by which the Supreme Being is known among any three West African peoples. [6 marks]
(b) Describe three attributes of the Supreme Being in West African belief, illustrating each with a name, proverb or saying. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: any three correct names, 2 marks each - Yoruba Olodumare/Olorun; Igbo Chukwu/Chineke; Akan Onyame/Onyankopon; Ewe Mawu; Nupe Soko; Edo Osanobua
3 marks: creator (e.g. Chineke, 'God who creates')
3 marks: all-powerful ruler and king over the divinities, with illustration
3 marks: all-knowing, eternal, just, merciful or transcendent, with any suitable illustration
questions.explanation: Model answer: The Yoruba call God Olodumare or Olorun, the Igbo Chukwu or Chineke and the Akan Onyame. He is creator (Chineke), all-powerful and king over divinities, all-knowing, just and eternal; names and proverbs express these attributes.

questions.stem:
(a) Who are the ancestors in West African Traditional Religion? [3 marks]
(b) State four qualifications for becoming an ancestor. [8 marks]
(c) Give two ways in which the living honour the ancestors. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: departed members of the family/community who lived good lives and are believed to live on in the spirit world, caring for the living
8 marks: any four, 2 marks each - lived to old age; good moral life; had children; died a natural/good death; received proper burial rites; was a member of the lineage
4 marks: any two, 2 marks each - libation and prayers; sacrifices and offerings; festivals such as Adae or Egungun; naming children after them; keeping ancestral shrines/stools
questions.explanation: Model answer: Ancestors are the honoured dead of a lineage who remain part of the family. To qualify one must live long and uprightly, have children, die naturally and be properly buried. They are honoured through libation, offerings, festivals and the care of ancestral shrines or stools.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the main activities that take place at a naming ceremony in any West African society you have studied. [9 marks]
(b) State three reasons why naming ceremonies are important in W.A.T.R. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
9 marks: any three activities described, 3 marks each - gathering of family on the appointed day; prayers and libation; use of symbolic items (water, salt, honey, kola, pepper) with meaning; announcing names chosen by elders/parents; presenting the baby to the community; feasting and gifts
6 marks: any three, 2 marks each - welcomes child as member of the community; gives identity; names express circumstances/hopes; links child to ancestors; blessing and protection
questions.explanation: Model answer: On the appointed day relatives gather; an elder prays and pours libation; symbolic items such as water, salt, honey and kola are touched to the baby's lips with wishes for a sweet, peaceful life; the names are announced and the baby presented to all, followed by feasting. The rite gives identity, welcomes the child into the community and invokes blessing and protection.

questions.topic: The Role of W.A.T.R. in Conflict Resolution and Management
questions.stem:
(a) Explain three ways by which W.A.T.R. helps to settle disputes in the community. [9 marks]
(b) Give three reasons why these methods are becoming less effective today. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
9 marks: any three explained, 3 marks each - oath-taking before a divinity; trial by ordeal; settlement by council of elders/chief; divination to find the truth; sacrifice for reconciliation
6 marks: any three, 2 marks each - influence of Christianity and Islam; modern courts and police; Western education/scepticism; urban migration; abuse by some priests
questions.explanation: Model answer: Disputing parties may swear an oath before a divinity such as Ogun, accept an ordeal, or appear before elders and chiefs who rely on tradition and divination; reconciliation is sealed with sacrifice. These means weaken as people embrace other faiths, use courts and police, move to cities and doubt traditional sanctions.

questions.stem:
(a) Give an account of Godianism as a new religious movement in Nigeria. [8 marks]
(b) Suggest four factors that may help W.A.T.R. to survive in the modern world. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: founded in Nigeria by K. O. K. Onyioha
3 marks: seeks to revive and organise belief in the God of African forefathers, rejecting the idea that foreign religions are the only path
3 marks: features such as organised meetings/worship, emphasis on African identity and culture, nationalist outlook
2 marks: first factor - cultural revival through festivals
2 marks: second factor - tourism to sacred sites and festivals
2 marks: third factor - academic study and government recognition
1 mark: fourth factor - research into herbal medicine or adaptation to modern forms
questions.explanation: Model answer: Godianism was founded by K. O. K. Onyioha to promote worship of the God of Africa's forefathers in an organised form, stressing African identity against the dominance of imported faiths. W.A.T.R. may survive through cultural festivals, tourism, academic study, research into herbal medicine and readiness to adapt.
